source.title: CRSSC: Salvage Reusable Samples from Noisy Data for Robust Learning
source.authors: Ze-Ren Sun; Xian-Sheng Hua; Ya-Zhou Yao; Xiu-Shen Wei; Guosheng Hu; Jian Zhang

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper; no truncation or garbling prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports a noisy-CIFAR100 experiment tracking prediction accuracy over training for clean and mislabeled samples, bearing on whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy labels. It does not reproduce the original random-labeling setup.
record.gate_note: The paper cites memorization results from prior work, which are not rows. Its own Figure 8 reports prediction-accuracy curves for a baseline and CRSSC on synthetic Noisy-CIFAR100; the text does not provide exact curve values.
record.test_reason: Section 5.9 reports the baseline ResNet-18's own training dynamics on synthetic Noisy-CIFAR100: clean samples are learned initially and noisy samples are eventually fitted. This bears on V6 in a new setting, although the paper primarily develops a mitigation method.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes Section 5.9: the baseline eventually fits noisy data, whereas CRSSC suppresses this overfitting and makes better use of mislabeled samples through relabeling. The paper's broader conclusion is that salvaging hard and mislabeled samples improves robustness and webly supervised fine-grained classification performance.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a synthetic noisy-label classification experiment and tracks per-group prediction accuracy over training; it does not apply the original study's complete random-labeling experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome differs between the baseline ResNet-18 and CRSSC training procedure.

fits_no_version.finding: CRSSC suppresses fitting of corrupted labels while preserving clean-sample learning through sample selection and relabeling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sample selection and label correction can reduce memorization of corrupted labels during noisy-data training.

record.problems: Figure 8 provides curves without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The synthetic setup corrupts 20% of selected samples and includes irrelevant categories, so it does not test fully random labels on the whole training set.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results bearing on the listed versions were identified. Other figures and tables concern CRSSC sample selection, label correction, parameter sensitivity, or benchmark accuracy rather than these claim versions.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for true and random labels, and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
A corruption sweep from none to all, perfect training fit throughout, and steadily increasing test error toward chance.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Fully random labeling and generality beyond the baseline ResNet-18 in this mixed clean, mislabeled, and irrelevant-category setting.

record.verdict_notes: The CRSSC results do not warrant a limits_scope verdict on V6: preventing memorization through a deliberately modified training procedure does not establish a failure of the ordinary-training learning order. Figure 8's caption identifies corrupted-label and ground-truth scoring, but the supplied text does not expose numerical curves.

versions.untested_parts: The paper corrupts 20% of selected training samples and treats 20 categories as irrelevant; it does not test a completely random labeling of the entire training set or report fitting it to zero error.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.
No sweep from clean labels to fully corrupted labels measuring training and test error.
No test of whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
The experiment uses 20% corrupted labels and irrelevant categories, not fully random labels across the training set; it does not establish the claim for standard networks generally.

conditions.value: prediction accuracy on clean training samples

rows.note: The figure shows the clean-sample accuracy curve; the text says CRSSC suppresses overfitting to noise and preserves classification ability.
rows.check: Clean-sample accuracy under CRSSC measures the mitigation method's learning performance; it does not establish clean-before-noise learning. Remove its V6 link.

rows.subject: CRSSC model
rows.operation_detail: Train CRSSC on synthetic Noisy-CIFAR100 and track prediction accuracy over training.

conditions.value: mislabeled samples, scored against corrupted labels

rows.note: The text says overfitting to noise is effectively suppressed, while relabeling lets mislabeled samples be learned using their correct labels.
rows.check: CRSSC deliberately selects samples and replaces labels to suppress noise fitting. Accuracy against the original corrupted labels measures mitigation effectiveness, not whether ordinary training learns real patterns before noise. The partial state for V6 is unwarranted.
